subject: 2D71B43F6FD6403083AC1BCB025C195E
introduction: “The pages of swiftly-appearing newspapers are indeed the mirror of the world.” Bahá’u’lláh praised the press in the 1880s and in the same passage asked that it be “purged from the promptings of evil passions” and investigate before it prints; He Himself had been slandered in it. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá told American editors that they were the guardians of human rights, and that a newspaper’s first duty is truth and its second harmony. Most of the guide is correspondence about particular papers. The Qur’an’s “verify it” and Exodus’s “false report” are the old rule for news; Milton’s Areopagitica and Mill’s On Liberty are the classic case for a free press, and they raise the question of what happens when truth and harmony pull apart.
questions: What duties do the readings lay on editors? Which is hardest to keep?
Reading 11 wants newspapers to create harmony. Milton wanted them free to quarrel. Can both be had?
How should a person who has been misreported respond, on the readings’ example?
What would “investigate before publishing” require of someone who shares news today?

outside.why: Newspapers are the mirror of the world. Milton, arguing for an unlicensed press: let Truth and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse, in a free and open encounter?
O newspapers! Have ye heard the moaning of the oppressed? Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
Some publish fabricated reports without investigation. If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent.
The Mosaic law put it among the first duties of a witness: thou shalt not raise a false report.
Every fact to be examined before publication. He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Publishers are guides of nations. Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Editors must spread the realities of facts. Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates.
Those that hold the mirror up to truth are like lights. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
What is concealed in hearts brought out. There is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.
Editors are the guardians of the rights of man. Mill: he who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.

A newspaper must first of all create harmony. James knew what public speech usually does: the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. Can a press both report conflict truthfully and serve harmony, and which gives way when they clash?
Milton feared the harmonious press more than the quarrelsome one: a man may be a heretic in the truth, if he believes things only because his pastor says so. Is a press that aims at unity still free?
A false report in wartime, and its cost. Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
Treatises published in London. What ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops.
One who seeks truth must recognize calumny for what it is. Answer not a fool according to his folly.

shortfall: The remaining fifty-five readings are letters about particular newspapers, articles and editors, which need no companion.
